Fit a mixture transition distribution (MTD) model

Source: R/fitMTD.R
fitMTD.Rd

Estimates by maximum likelihood the mixture transition distribution model of Raftery (1985) for a high-order Markov chain: the probability of the next state is a weighted mixture of the contributions of the last order states, all governed by the same transition matrix.

Usage

fitMTD(
  sequence,
  order = 2,
  start = NULL,
  nstart = 1,
  tol = 1e-10,
  maxit = 10000L,
  model = c("MTD", "MTDg"),
  accelerate = FALSE,
  se = FALSE,
  negativeWeights = FALSE
)

Arguments

sequence

An empirical sequence of states (a character vector, or a vector coercible to character), without missing values, or a list of such vectors, taken as independent sequences (see Details).

order

Order of the model, a positive integer smaller than the length of the sequence.

start

Index of the first observation entering the likelihood, at least order + 1 (the default).

nstart

nstart - 1 is the number of random starting points of the EM algorithm added to the deterministic ones (see Details).

tol

Convergence tolerance on the relative change of the log-likelihood between two iterations.

maxit

Maximum number of EM iterations for each starting point (EM steps, if accelerate = TRUE).

model

"MTD" (default), the model with a single matrix, or "MTDg", the general model with a different matrix for each lag.

accelerate

Logical: speed up the EM algorithm with the SQUAREM scheme of Varadhan and Roland (2008)? The default FALSE keeps the plain algorithm. Convergence is much faster when the likelihood is flat, and the same maximum is reached.

se

Logical: compute standard errors (see Details)?

negativeWeights

Logical: allow negative lag weights, as in Raftery (1985)? Only for model = "MTD"; the default FALSE keeps them non-negative.

Value

A list with components

lambda

the estimated lag weights, named lag1, lag2, ...

estimate

a markovchain object (by row) with the estimated transition matrix \(Q\) (for model = "MTDg", a list with the order objects of the matrices \(Q_1, \dots, Q_k\))

Q

a list of order copies of \(Q\) (the \(Q_g\) for "MTDg") stored by column (Q[[g]][to, from]), the layout returned by fitHigherOrder, so that the fit can be passed to higherOrderLogLik

X

the relative frequencies of the states in sequence

logLikelihood, npar, AIC, BIC, nobs

maximized log-likelihood, number of free parameters, information criteria and number of observations entering the likelihood

order, start

as used in the fit

iterations, converged

EM iterations (sweeps of the coordinate ascent with negativeWeights = TRUE) and convergence flag of the returned fit

model

"MTD" or "MTDg"

negativeWeights

as used in the fit

se

only if se = TRUE: a list with the standard errors lambda of the weights, Q of the matrix (same layout as estimate; NA for the entries that cannot be estimated and, for MTDg, for all the weights and matrices) and probabilities of the transition probabilities, a matrix with one row per history observed in the data (named by its states, oldest first, separated by "-", as passed to higherOrderPredict) and one column per next state; see Details

Details

For an order \(k\) the model is $$P(X_t = j \mid X_{t-1} = i_1, \dots, X_{t-k} = i_k) = \sum_{g=1}^{k} \lambda_g\, q_{i_g j},$$ where \(Q = (q_{ij})\) is an \(r \times r\) transition matrix (rows are departure states) and the lag weights \(\lambda_g\) sum to one. It needs \(r(r-1) + k - 1\) parameters instead of the \(r^k (r-1)\) of a fully parameterized Markov chain of order \(k\), which makes high orders practicable (Raftery, 1985; Berchtold and Raftery, 2002). This is different from the model fitted by fitHigherOrder, which mixes a different empirical matrix for each lag and does not estimate them jointly with the weights.

By default the weights are constrained to be non-negative, as in most applications of the model (see below for negative weights). Under this constraint the likelihood is maximized by the EM algorithm of Lebre and Bourguignon (2008), in which the latent variable is the lag that generated each observation; it is implemented in C++. Every iteration increases the likelihood, but the likelihood of the MTD model can have several local maxima (Berchtold, 2001). The models of order \(1, \dots,\) order are therefore fitted in turn on the same observations, and order \(k\) is started from equal weights with the transition matrix of all lags pooled, and from the fit of order \(k - 1\) extended with a zero and with a small positive weight for the new lag. The first of these extensions has the likelihood of order \(k - 1\), so the likelihood returned never decreases with the order, as it must for nested models. nstart - 1 further random starting points can be added for the requested order; they are drawn at random, so call set.seed beforehand for reproducible results. The fit with the highest likelihood is returned.

The likelihood is conditional on the observations before start: it is the product of the transition probabilities of \(x_t\) for \(t = \) start, \(\dots\), \(n\). The default, order + 1, uses every observation an order-order model can predict. To compare models of different orders (or with the Markov chains of fitHigherOrder via higherOrderLogLik) use the same start for all, for instance \(1 +\) the largest order; Berchtold and Raftery (2002) condition on the first 14 observations, i.e. start = 15.

With a list of sequences the likelihood is the product over the sequences: each contributes the observations from start to its end, the earlier ones being only used as conditioning states, no lag spans two sequences, and a sequence with fewer than start states is not used (apart from the state frequencies X). order must be smaller than the length of the longest sequence.

A state that never occurs in a conditioning position (for instance one observed only at the end of the sequence) does not enter the likelihood; its row of \(Q\) is not identified and is returned as uniform.

A warning is given when the number of observations entering the likelihood does not exceed the number of free parameters.

With model = "MTDg" (Berchtold, 2001; Lebre and Bourguignon, 2008) the probability of the next state is \(\sum_g \lambda_g\, q^{(g)}_{i_g j}\) with a transition matrix \(Q_g\) for each lag. It has \((r-1)(1 + k(r-1))\) free parameters, the number of the models of fitHigherOrder, of which it is the maximum likelihood version: there the matrices are the empirical ones and only the weights are fitted. The EM algorithm is the same; order \(k\) is started from the MTD fit of the same order, from the empirical matrices with the best weights for them, and from the fit of order \(k - 1\), so its likelihood is never below those of model = "MTD" and of the method = "mle" fit of fitHigherOrder, nor of lower orders. The row of \(Q_g\) of a state never seen at lag \(g\) is returned as uniform.

The weights and matrices of the MTDg model are not identified: since the probabilities only depend on the products \(A_g = \lambda_g Q_g\), adding \(\epsilon\) times the same probability vector to every row of \(A_1\) and subtracting it from every row of \(A_2\) changes \(\lambda_1\), \(\lambda_2\), \(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\) but no transition probability. The maximum is therefore attained on a set of dimension up to \((k - 1) r\), of which the values returned are one point; only the transition probabilities (and the likelihood) are determined, and npar counts the identified parameters. The lag weights of an MTDg fit should not be interpreted as the importance of the lags.

With negativeWeights = TRUE (model "MTD" only) the weights may be negative, as in Raftery's (1985) original formulation, provided every transition probability \(\sum_g \lambda_g q_{i_g j}\) lies in \([0, 1]\) for all the combinations of departure states \(i_g\): for each arrival state \(j\), \(\min_i q_{ij}\) times the sum of the positive weights must not be below \(\max_i q_{ij}\) times the sum of the absolute negative weights (Raftery, 1985). The EM algorithm does not apply, and the likelihood is maximized by block coordinate ascent in the spirit of Berchtold (2001): in the weights and in each row of \(Q\) in turn, mass is moved from the entry with the smallest to the one with the largest partial derivative, by the step that maximizes the likelihood along that direction within the feasible region. Order \(k\) starts from the fit with non-negative weights of the same order and from the fit of order \(k - 1\) with a zero weight for the new lag, so its likelihood is never below either of them; for the requested order it also starts with each lag in turn given a negative weight. The likelihood has several local maxima, and this is slower than the EM algorithm. iterations then counts the sweeps of the ascent at the requested order. Unidentified rows of \(Q\) are returned as uniform, or as the mean of the other rows if a uniform row would violate the condition.

With se = TRUE the standard errors are those of the observed information at the maximum, by the delta method, obtained in closed form with the entries of each probability vector (the weights and each row of \(Q\)) summing to one. Entries that are on the boundary of the parameter space (below \(10^{-4}\)) are held fixed, as in the usual treatment of constrained maxima, and have NA; a warning is given if a weight is among them, since then the standard errors of the others are conditional on that weight being zero (with negative weights allowed, if Raftery's condition is binding). Standard errors are also given for the transition probabilities of every history observed in the data. For the MTDg model only these are available, the weights and matrices not being identified; they are computed with a generalized inverse of the information, which gives the same variance for any identified quantity. All are asymptotic, and approximate in small samples or with sparse \(Q\).

AIC and BIC use the number of free parameters \(r(r-1) + k - 1\), and BIC the number of observations entering the likelihood. Berchtold and Raftery (2002) do not count the elements of \(Q\) estimated as exactly zero; their BIC can be obtained by subtracting the number of those elements from npar.

References

Raftery, A. E. (1985). A model for high-order Markov chains. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series B, 47(3), 528-539.

Berchtold, A. (2001). Estimation in the mixture transition distribution model. Journal of Time Series Analysis, 22(4), 379-397.

Berchtold, A. and Raftery, A. E. (2002). The mixture transition distribution model for high-order Markov chains and non-Gaussian time series. Statistical Science, 17(3), 328-356.

Lebre, S. and Bourguignon, P.-Y. (2008). An EM algorithm for estimation in the mixture transition distribution model. Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation, 78(1), 1-15.

Varadhan, R. and Roland, C. (2008). Simple and globally convergent methods for accelerating the convergence of any EM algorithm. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics, 35(2), 335-353.

See also

fitHigherOrder, higherOrderLogLik, higherOrderPredict, markovchainFit

Examples

# hourly wind directions at Koeberg (Berchtold and Raftery, 2002)
wind <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "koeberg_wind.csv",
                             package = "markovchain"))$state
fit <- fitMTD(wind, order = 2, start = 15)
fit$lambda
#>      lag1      lag2 
#> 0.7568342 0.2431658 
fit$estimate
#> MTD(2) 
#>  A  4 - dimensional discrete Markov Chain defined by the following states: 
#>  1, 2, 3, 4 
#>  The transition matrix  (by rows)  is defined as follows: 
#>            1          2          3            4
#> 1 0.83067002 0.06867021 0.00767778 9.298199e-02
#> 2 0.03699661 0.90114666 0.06185673 7.502067e-55
#> 3 0.01535363 0.15522884 0.80712064 2.229689e-02
#> 4 0.07788932 0.00000000 0.05271010 8.694006e-01
#> 
c(logLik = fit$logLikelihood, BIC = fit$BIC)
#>    logLik       BIC 
#> -393.3968  872.5032 

# several starting points guard against local maxima
set.seed(1)
fitMTD(wind, order = 3, start = 15, nstart = 5)$logLikelihood
#> [1] -393.2398

# standard errors, and the model with a matrix for each lag
fit2 <- fitMTD(wind, order = 2, start = 15, se = TRUE)
fit2$se$lambda
#>       lag1       lag2 
#> 0.05006497 0.05006497 
fitMTD(wind, order = 2, start = 15, model = "MTDg")$logLikelihood
#> [1] -389.4452
